trust_boundaries.name: Untrusted content into the model context

remit_rules.excerpt: content retrieved from external sources — web pages, emails, chat or integration messages, file contents, tool or MCP outputs — as trusted instructions; such content is data to be processed
MUST NOT accept or act on instructions from anyone other than its single owner-operator

threats.summary: A stranger messaging the agent over a connected platform gets a session opened and their text treated as a task — answered in code by the external_event gate, which returns before any session, trigger or action-selection LLM, with third-party as the default classification for unlabeled inbound.

The notification the gate posts still carries a 500-character preview of the stranger's message into CONVERSATION_HISTORY.md, so attacker-authored prose is in the model's context on the owner's next turn.

Page text from web_fetch, file contents and MCP tool output enter the context with no provenance label or trust tier; the one module named for input sanitization has no call site and returns matched text unchanged (checked: app/security/prompt_sanitizer.py:71, agent_core/core/impl/context/engine.py — no labeling or quarantine step).

remit_rules.excerpt: Stored credentials, OAuth/bot tokens, and LLM API keys MUST NEVER be printed to chat, written to logs, or transmitted to any destination.

threats.summary: Because the file actions accept any absolute path, the contents of .credentials/<platform>.json and settings.json can be read into the prompt and transmitted verbatim to the provider endpoint — no redaction or exclusion runs on the context-assembly path.

An unbounded action or retry loop burns the owner's provider spend — answered by the per-task action and token caps that pause the task behind a Continue/Abort choice, and by the five-failure circuit breaker in the LLM interface.

remit_rules.excerpt: Host command and code execution MUST be gated by owner approval and MUST NOT inherit the parent process environment containing provider API keys or other credentials
sandboxed code and shell execution; web search and fetch; document reading and generation; memory search; the actions exposed by external integrations the owner has connected
The agent MUST NOT auto-approve, self-grant, or downgrade the approval requirement for any action above its declared permission tier.

threats.summary: Model output travels one hop from unlabeled retrieved content to run_shell, which passes the string to the host shell with shell=True and env=os.environ.copy(), handing the inherited provider API keys to whatever the command does.

No approval mechanism exists anywhere on the dispatch path: permission_tier is range-validated at app/proactive/parser.py:321 and displayed but never read before an action runs, and add_action_sets is itself a core action the model uses to widen its own inventory mid-task.

In the documented Docker deployment the agent container that runs those shell commands has /var/run/docker.sock bind-mounted, so a model-authored command controls the host daemon and the container boundary confines nothing.

remit_rules.excerpt: Any irreversible or externally-visible action — sending a message, email, or post to an external recipient; deleting data; making a purchase or payment; or changing configuration or credentials — requires explicit owner approval before execution.
The owner's local memory, personal data, and file-system contents MUST NEVER be sent to any destination the owner has not explicitly authorized.

threats.summary: All 77 actions flagged irreversible=True — send_message plus the per-platform senders — execute against an arbitrary external recipient with no confirmation; the flag drives only the idempotency ledger, which deduplicates a repeat but never asks the owner.

http_request will POST an arbitrary body to any public host, so local file and memory contents can leave for a destination the owner never connected; the SSRF filter bounds only private, loopback and metadata addresses and places no limit on public destinations.

trust_boundaries.name: Persisted state re-entering the agent's reasoning

remit_rules.excerpt: The agent MUST NOT directly edit harness-managed state files — distilled memory, the append-only event log, conversation history, task history, and the memory index
MUST NOT redefine, expand, or weaken its own governance — its goals, permission tiers, approval gates, or safety decision rubric

threats.summary: write_file and stream_edit accept any absolute path with no protected-path denylist, so SOUL.md, AGENT.md and MEMORY.md — loaded into context at the start of every session — can be rewritten, making an injected instruction persist into every future session; the only protection is prose in AGENT.md:861 and the MEMORY.md header.

The ChromaDB index re-ingests agent-written markdown whenever the file watcher sees a change, with no validation, no hidden-content screening and no provenance field, so fetched external text can be retrieved by memory_search in a later session and read as the agent's own remembered knowledge.

trust_boundaries.name: Local stores readable into model context

remit_rules.excerpt: credential and configuration stores MUST be excluded from indexing, retrieval, and summarization by default
Credentials and tokens at rest MUST be stored with owner-only access and MUST NOT be world-readable.

threats.summary: read_file, grep_files and find_files take absolute host paths and check only that the file exists, so the OAuth tokens in .credentials/<platform>.json and the API keys in app/config/settings.json read straight into the model's context (checked: app/data/action/read_file.py:134 — no containment check, no exclusion list).

A separate reader reaches the same files: the default-enabled filesystem MCP server is launched with a '.' scope covering the whole repository, so its tools serve the configuration and credential paths as well as the workspace.
Another local account reads the stored tokens off disk — answered by the credential store, which chmods its directory 0700 and each credential file 0600 on write.

remit_rules.excerpt: No user-data token, bot token, or server-side API key may be embedded or shipped in the distributed code.
Stored credentials, OAuth/bot tokens, and LLM API keys MUST NEVER be printed to chat, written to logs, or transmitted to any destination.

threats.summary: Live client_id and client_secret values for five providers plus Telegram api_id and api_hash ship in the distributed source as base64 fragments joined at runtime, with the module docstring stating they are split to evade GitHub scanning and build helpers provided to make more.
Provider API keys supplied at start-up (env_file .env in the documented compose stack) cross into every shell child, because run_shell hands each command a full copy of the parent environment.

remit_rules.excerpt: Any server or skill enabled without an explicit owner action MUST be named here and version-pinned; a server whose launch resolves an unpinned upstream package on each start is outside this closure

threats.summary: Both default-enabled MCP servers resolve unpinned upstream packages on every start — npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem with no version and @playwright/mcp@latest — with no lockfile, hash or signed manifest, and their tools register directly as agent actions.

requirements.txt declares 55 packages with zero exact pins and no lockfile anywhere in the tree, so two installs can resolve different LLM SDK, vector-store and browser-automation code with no inventory to check a disclosed CVE against.
Sharing a Living UI fetches the cloudflared binary from a mutable GitHub 'latest' URL and executes it with no checksum, signature or version pin.

remit_rules.excerpt: Any server or listener the agent starts (OAuth callback server, Living UI applications, integration bridges) MUST bind to loopback/localhost and MUST NOT be exposed to the public network without explicit owner approval.

threats.summary: The Living UI sidecar proxy binds 0.0.0.0 with wildcard CORS and no auth dependency, and every scaffolded backend inherits the same bind from the template, so anyone on the same LAN can reach the bridge the agent uses to read and act on Living UI data.

The GUI desktop service publishes port 3001 on all host interfaces with a literal default password and seccomp:unconfined, handing anyone who reaches it a graphical session on the machine the agent operates.
The OAuth callback listener is the one server that answers this boundary in code — it binds 127.0.0.1 explicitly for the consent round-trip.

remit_rules.excerpt: Routine actions and decisions MUST be recorded to the durable event/action log for audit, without interrupting the owner.
Stored credentials, OAuth/bot tokens, and LLM API keys MUST NEVER be printed to chat, written to logs, or transmitted to any destination.

threats.summary: Every loguru sink is added with backtrace=True and diagnose=True, so a propagating exception renders local variables — including provider keys and OAuth tokens on the integration and LLM call paths — into the log file, and no sink installs a redaction filter.

Recording is strong but nothing notifies: the irreversible-action ledger and the structured logs stay on local disk with no alert hook and no exporter, and a compromise holding host shell access can edit the same files it would be detected by.

notes.lane_fit: Two placements strained. The Living UI subsystem is one capability with two faces — an agent tool and a set of 0.0.0.0 listeners — and was kept in tools_mcp as the tool the model drives, with its network exposure carried on the control-plane-exposure boundary rather than split into a second external_deploy node. The CraftOS platform connector is genuinely bidirectional (inbound listeners and the outbound send facade live in the same package) and sits in client_adapters as a channel connector for both directions.
notes.omissions: Arbitration divergences from the stored tags, KB-first. Substantive: PRAX-2026-08-12-007 is stored ASI02 (Tool Misuse) but no wrongful use is evidenced — under the Agentic KB's arbitration the ungated-approval half is LLM03 (Excessive Agency) and the unbounded-destination half is LLM02 (Sensitive Information Disclosure), so its two threats are tagged that way here. Precedence-only: PRAX-2026-08-12-003 carries both LLM03 and ASI10 in the findings JSON; the compound row makes LLM03 primary with ASI10 riding as a co-tag, so the single owasp field takes LLM03. Two threats are tagged null (the observability gap at telemetry-egress and the file-permission threat at data-at-rest) because neither Top 10 honestly applies. Size discipline (12-25 nodes) meant three cited artifacts are represented only as boundary threats rather than as nodes of their own: requirements.txt (PRAX-2026-08-12-012), the cloudflared download URL table (PRAX-2026-08-12-013, cited on the Living UI node), and the app/usage SQLite stores (folded into the observability node's evidence). Two nodes are deliberately edgeless: the PromptSanitizer stub (dead code, no call site to draw an edge from) and the Docker deployment stack (deploy posture). Sub-agents were checked and are in-process only (app/subagent/runner.py, spawn_subagent), with no network agent-to-agent protocol, so no peer-a2a boundary was raised. The remit's R-13 names prewarm_all_drives as the whole-machine indexing feature; no such symbol exists anywhere in this snapshot, so the drive-prewarm mechanism could not be cited and no node was created for it.
